name: Ramelteon

lead: Ramelteon is a prescription drug for trouble falling asleep. It works on the same receptors as the body's own melatonin rather than on the GABA system.
Trials show it shortens the time to fall asleep by roughly 10 to 19 minutes versus placebo. No studies have examined it for appearance outcomes.

paras: It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors thought to be involved in the sleep-wake rhythm, and is quickly cleared from the body.

Labelled adverse effects include somnolence, dizziness, fatigue and nausea, with rare allergic reactions and complex sleep behaviours. It is Rx-only in the US, not a controlled substance, and not authorised in the EU.

lead: Ramelteon is a prescription melatonin receptor agonist taken by mouth for insomnia characterised by difficulty falling asleep. It binds the MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors and, according to its US label, has no appreciable affinity for the GABA receptor complex used by benzodiazepines and Z-drugs [1][2]. It was approved by the US FDA in 2005 under the brand name Rozerem and is not a controlled substance in the United States [1].

In the wiki's recovery category it is listed as a sleep-related compound. No published study has examined ramelteon for any appearance outcome, and no looksmaxxing community material about it was identified. Its documented use is medical.

Trials report small reductions in the time taken to fall asleep compared with placebo. The European Medicines Agency has not authorised it [1]. The 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline and later network meta-analyses place it among several insomnia drug options with modest effects [3][4].
infobox: Rx-only; not a controlled substance in the US [1]

paras: The US label indicates ramelteon for insomnia characterised by difficulty with sleep onset, with supporting trials up to six months long [2]. Reviews of the trial data describe reductions in latency to persistent sleep on the order of 10 to 19 minutes versus placebo, with smaller gains in total sleep time [1]. Phase 3 programmes enrolled adults and elderly people with chronic insomnia and healthy volunteers with transient insomnia [5][6][7].

Ramelteon has also been studied in delayed sleep phase syndrome and jet lag, and in a randomised placebo-controlled trial for prevention of delirium in hospitalised older patients [8][9][10]. Those uses are not part of the US label.

The most common reactions listed on the label (at least 3% and more frequent than placebo) are somnolence, dizziness, fatigue, nausea and worsened insomnia [2]. Warnings cover rare angioedema and anaphylaxis, complex sleep behaviours such as sleep-driving, worsening depression, and possible effects on reproductive hormones such as prolactin and testosterone [1][2]. Co-use with fluvoxamine is contraindicated because it raises ramelteon exposure [1].

Ramelteon acts as an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors, which are thought to be involved in the circadian rhythm that underlies the sleep-wake cycle [2][11]. It is rapidly absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism mainly by the CYP1A2 enzyme and has a short elimination half-life of about 1 to 2.6 hours [1].
Ramelteon is available only by prescription in the US and has not been authorised in the European Union [1]. The wiki found no community discussion of ramelteon as a looksmaxxing compound.

Registered phase 3 trials of ramelteon in chronic insomnia enrolled 405 to 1,213 participants each, including an elderly-only trial of 829 participants [5][12][13]. A phase 2 trial examined delayed sleep phase syndrome and a phase 4 trial examined jet-lag insomnia [8][9]. A 2014 randomised placebo-controlled trial in JAMA Psychiatry reported less delirium with ramelteon in acutely ill older patients [10]. Guideline and network meta-analysis authors characterise its effect on sleep onset as small [3][4]. No studies were found on ramelteon for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Approved by the US FDA as the first prescription drug of its melatonin-agonist class [1].
The European Medicines Agency concluded the evidence did not show benefits outweighing risks, and it was not authorised there [1].
A randomised trial reported lower delirium incidence with ramelteon in hospitalised older patients [10].
